knowledge_point.title: Rewriting a Double Integral Over a Circle or Part-Circle Centered at the Origin

question.:question/problem:
![](images/7b/7bd61d778e3ea17a10adad21dd63cfae068af48700e6217194bb48e995c9f6e7.png)

The region $D$ is the circle shown above. What is ${∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A$ expressed in polar coordinates?

Choose a change-of-variables setup with $r\geq0$ that describes $D$ and the transformed integrand, including the Jacobian.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA={∬}_{Δ}\,f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\,dr\,d\theta .
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents the disk of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ the region can be expressed as 

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\leq r\leq \sqrt{2},\ 0\leq\theta\leq 2 \pi\}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{Δ}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}-(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{r}^{3}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}{r}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡2\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

generation.response_criterion: valid change-of-variables setup for actual D, with nonnegative r and transformed integrand times Jacobian

question.:question/problem:
![](images/b4/b4a332a1bea58e47ab58fa47c6944213ce4caa5d26e6bfb129fea613adcd524b.png)

The region $D$ is the quarter-circle shown above. What is $\iint_D 2 x y \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}A$ expressed in polar coordinates?

Choose a change-of-variables setup with $r\geq0$ that describes $D$ and the transformed integrand, including the Jacobian.
question.:question/worked-solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
\iint_D f(x,y)\,\mathrm{d}A=\iint_\Delta f(r\cos\theta,r\sin\theta)\,r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta.
$$

First, notice that the region $D$ represents a portion of the disk of radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin. In polar coordinates $(r,\theta),$ the region can be expressed as

$$
\Delta=\{(r,\theta):0\leq r\leq \sqrt{2},\ 0\leq\theta\leq \frac{\pi}{2}\}.
$$

Since $r\geq0$, $\sqrt{r^2}=r$; also $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$.

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\iint_D 2 x y \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\,\mathrm{d}A&=\iint_\Delta 2 (r\cos\theta) (r\sin\theta) \sqrt{(r\cos\theta)^{2} + (r\sin\theta)^{2}}\,r\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}2r^3\cos\theta\sin\theta\sqrt{r^2(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta)}\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}2r^4\cos\theta\sin\theta\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta \\ &=\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{2}}r^4\sin(2\theta)\,\mathrm{d}r\,\mathrm{d}\theta\end{aligned}
$$

$$
